summary: Describes version 3 of the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TPv3). It defines the base control protocol and an encapsulation for tunneling multiple Layer 2 connections between two IP nodes. Separate documents give the details for each link type being emulated.

eli5.summary: It builds a hidden tunnel through the Internet so two faraway networks act as though they were plugged into the same cable.

subtitle: How to tunnel Layer 2 circuits such as Ethernet or PPP across an IP network with a control channel and a lightweight data header.

tldr.problem: Layer 2 connections (PPP, Ethernet, Frame Relay and others) needed a standard way to be carried between two points across a packet network, and the earlier L2TP was tied closely to PPP.
tldr.mechanism: L2TPv3 defines a reliable control protocol that sets up and tears down sessions between two endpoints, and a data encapsulation with a 32-bit Session ID, optional Cookie and optional sublayer, sent directly over IP or over UDP.
tldr.outcome: It separates the base protocol from the payload type, so each link type is described in its own companion document. It has been updated by RFC 5641 and RFC 9601.

today: RFC 3931 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5641 and RFC 9601, so read it together with those documents. It builds on the PPP-focused RFC 2661.

sections.title: Introduction and Changes from L2TPv2
sections.content:
The Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) provides a dynamic mechanism for tunneling Layer 2 (L2) circuits across a packet-oriented network such as IP. As first defined in RFC 2661 it carried Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) sessions, and it has since been adopted for other L2 protocols. RFC 3931 describes the base protocol on its own, independent of the L2 payload.

The base protocol has two parts: a control protocol for creating, maintaining and tearing down sessions, and a data encapsulation that multiplexes and demultiplexes L2 data streams between two nodes. Separate documents are expected for each emulated link type, called a pseudowire type (PPP, Ethernet, Frame Relay and so on).

The notable changes from L2TPv2 are the removal of PPP-specific constructs, a move from 16-bit to 32-bit identifiers (Session ID and Control Connection ID), and authentication that covers the whole control message instead of part of it.
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook for building a pretend cable through the Internet. It can carry many kinds of traffic, and each kind gets its own extra rules in another book.

sections.title: Topology and Terminology
sections.content:
L2TP runs between two L2TP Control Connection Endpoints (LCCEs). An LCCE that connects a session directly to a data link is called an L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC). One that ends the session and processes the encapsulated network layer packet on a virtual interface is an L2TP Network Server (LNS). One node can be an LAC for some sessions and an LNS for others.

The RFC names three tunneling models: LAC-LNS, LAC-LAC and LNS-LNS. In LAC-LAC, each LAC acts as a simple cross-connect between a circuit and an L2TP session, and either side may start a session, with a tie-breaking mechanism if both do at once.

Two more terms matter throughout. A control connection is the reliable channel used to set up and release sessions. A session is the entity created between two LCCEs to maintain one emulated L2 connection, and one control connection can carry several sessions. There is one pseudowire per session.
sections.eli5: Imagine two post offices linked by a private road. Each office can hand over letters from its own town or pass them on, and the road can carry many separate bundles at once.

sections.title: Control and Data Messages
sections.content:
L2TP has two kinds of messages. Control messages travel over a reliable control channel. Data messages carry the L2 traffic over an unreliable data channel and are not retransmitted when packets are lost.

The control message header has the T bit (set to 1), the L and S bits (both set to 1), a Ver field set to 3, a Length, a 32-bit Control Connection ID, and the sequence numbers Ns and Nr. Reserved bits MUST be 0 when sent and ignored on receipt. Connection IDs have local significance only, so the ID in a message is the one chosen by the intended recipient.

A data message is a session header, an optional L2-specific sublayer and the tunnel payload. The default sublayer has an S bit and a 24-bit sequence number, which can detect lost, duplicate or out-of-order packets. Messages inside control are identified by type: for example SCCRQ is 1, SCCRP is 2, SCCCN is 3, StopCCN is 4, HELLO is 6, ICRQ is 10, ICRP is 11, ICCN is 12, CDN is 14 and ACK is 20. The details of each message are carried in Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs), which have a 10-bit length field, so one AVP carries at most 1023 octets.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of notes. Important notes about setting things up get a receipt and are re-sent if lost. The notes carrying the real traffic are just dropped in the mail with no receipt.

sections.title: Carrying Data over IP or UDP
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support L2TP directly over IP, which uses IP protocol number 115, and SHOULD support L2TP over UDP for better NAT and firewall traversal and easier migration from L2TPv2. Over UDP, control messages MUST use UDP port 1701, and UDP checksums MUST be enabled for control messages but MAY be disabled for data.

Every data message carries a 32-bit Session ID, which identifies the session at the receiver, and an optional Cookie of up to 64 bits. After looking up the session by Session ID, the receiver checks the Cookie against the value signaled during setup, and packets with an invalid Session ID or Cookie MUST be dropped. Over IP, the Session ID of zero is reserved for control messages. Over UDP, the T bit tells control from data.

The RFC also covers fragmentation. An implementation MUST implement at least one method for managing mismatched MTUs, such as fragmenting before encapsulation or fragmenting the resulting L2TP/IP packet. The data channel offers no cryptographic security, so if it crosses an untrusted network, IPsec MUST be made available.
sections.eli5: Each bundle of traffic gets a ticket number saying which tunnel it belongs to, plus a secret password stamp. If the number or stamp is wrong, the bundle is thrown away.

sections.title: Reliable Control Delivery and Keepalive
sections.content:
Control messages get a reliable service built on a sliding window. Ns is a counter that starts at 0 and wraps at 65536, and Nr carries the number of the next message expected. All control messages except the ACK consume a sequence number. Duplicates are ignored but MUST be acknowledged, in case the earlier ACK was lost.

An unacknowledged message is retransmitted after a recommended default of 1 second, and each further retransmission MUST use exponential backoff (1, 2, 4 seconds and so on). A cap on the interval SHOULD be no less than 8 seconds. After several retransmissions, with a recommended default of 10 that MUST be configurable, the control connection and all its sessions MUST be cleared. A peer states its limit with the Receive Window Size AVP, and a sender MUST NOT exceed it. The RFC recommends a slow start and congestion avoidance procedure, described in Appendix A.

To detect lost connectivity, an LCCE MUST send a Hello if a period of time passes without receiving any message from the peer. The recommended default is 60 seconds, and it MUST be configurable. If a Hello is not reliably delivered, the control connection is declared down.
sections.eli5: The setup notes work like registered mail. If the other side does not confirm, you send again, waiting a bit longer each time, and eventually give up. If it is quiet for a while, you send a quick hello to check they are still there.

sections.title: Setting Up Connections and Sessions
sections.content:
A control connection is established with a three-message exchange: SCCRQ (Start-Control-Connection-Request), SCCRP (the reply) and SCCCN (Connected). It is torn down by either side sending a single StopCCN. The recipient MUST acknowledge it and keep enough state to accept retransmissions, with at least 31 seconds recommended for a full retransmission cycle.

Once the control connection is up, sessions are created with another three-message exchange. For an incoming call it is ICRQ, ICRP, ICCN. For an outgoing call it is OCRQ, OCRP, OCCN. Either side tears a session down with a single CDN. After the last session is cleared, the control connection MAY be torn down too.

The state machines in section 7 define what each side does on every message. The control connection has four states: idle, wait-ctl-reply, wait-ctl-conn and established. If both sides send an SCCRQ at once, the Control Connection Tie Breaker AVP decides which wins.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone call with a handshake: one side says hello, the other answers, and the first confirms. Then they can start separate conversations inside the call, and ending any of them takes one short message.

sections.title: Authentication, Cookies and IPsec
sections.content:
Control Message Authentication is optional. It uses a one-way hash over the entire control message, a pre-configured shared secret and a nonce from each side. It provides mutual endpoint authentication and a per-message integrity check, and it guards against spoofing and replay. It is always bidirectional, and the shared secret never needs to be sent in the clear. If IPsec already protects the traffic, it can be disabled when both peers agree. Hidden AVPs (the H bit) can keep values such as passwords from travelling as cleartext.

For data packets, the Session ID and Cookie give traffic separation between VPNs. For protection against brute-force blind insertion attacks, a 64-bit Cookie MUST be used with all sessions, because a 32-bit Cookie is vulnerable to brute-force guessing at high packet rates. Cookies MUST be chosen in a cryptographically random manner. The Cookie gives no protection against an attacker who can sniff and correlate traffic, so over an untrusted network IPsec should be used instead.
sections.eli5: The tunnel ends can prove who they are using a secret password without ever shouting it out loud. Each bundle also carries a hard-to-guess code so strangers cannot slip fake bundles in.

sections.title: Migrating from L2TPv2
sections.content:
L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 are meant to coexist during migration. Over IP only, with no need to talk to L2TPv2, an implementation can mostly ignore migration issues. Over UDP, L2TPv3 uses the same port 1701 and shares the first two octets of the header format with L2TPv2, so the Ver field is used to tell them apart.

Automatic fallback works by sending an SCCRQ with its Ver field set to 2, with every L2TPv3-specific AVP having the M bit set to 0 so an L2TPv2-only peer ignores them. If the peer answers with Ver set to 3, operation continues as L2TPv3. If it answers with Ver 2, the peer is assumed to be L2TPv2-only and the implementation falls back. There is no deterministic fallback from L2TPv3 over IP.
sections.eli5: The new tunnel speaks a slightly different language from the old one. The first message is worded so that both kinds of listeners understand it, and the answer shows which language to keep using.
